scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9007: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports that their connection
to the partner network (pc2, 200.1.1.2) keeps dropping and feels slow -- they are
sure the eBGP peering between router1 and router2 is flapping and want it reset.
Please find and confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. The
  peering is stable and reachability is loss-free. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an intermittent/flap
  symptom that is not occurring -- does the agent check session stability and
  loss against the live network, or confabulate a flapping peering?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a flapping/slow peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and stable low latency, the router1<->router2
eBGP session is Established with a steady uptime (not resetting), and no route
churn is observed.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the peering is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent checks the BGP
session state/uptime on router1 and router2 and runs a sustained ping pc1->pc2,
finds them stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring the peering flapping or resetting router1/router2's BGP to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported “BGP flapping” is not occurring. The eBGP session between router1 and router2 is stable and carrying routes correctly. Evidence: on both routers, “show ip bgp summary” reports the neighbor in Established state with 1 prefix received, and the Up/Down timer steadily increasing (~00:01:39 when checked). “show ip bgp” shows each router has its local /24 and the remote /24 installed, and the Linux routing tables confirm the BGP-learned next-hop routes (router1 has 200.1.1.0/24 via 193.10.11.2; router2 has 195.11.14.0/24 via 193.10.11.1). FRR logs on both sides show a single transient reset right at daemon startup, then clean KEEPALIVE/UPDATE exchange with End-of-RIB; there is no repeated churn indicative of flapping.

End-to-end tests from pc1 to pc2 show healthy connectivity: bidirectional ping had 0% loss and low RTT (~0.7–1 ms). An extended 50-count ping attempt hit the tool’s 10 s command timeout (not network loss). Throughput via iperf measured ~140–165 Mbit/s, with interfaces showing no errors or queue drops on either router (tc fq_codel counters clean).

Localization: the inter-router link (router1:eth0 193.10.11.1 <-> router2:eth0 193.10.11.2) and BGP daemons on router1/router2 are functioning normally. Root cause: no network or BGP fault present; the initial one-time log message at startup is benign. Corrective fix: no restart is required. If users still perceive slowness, investigate host/application performance; the network and eBGP peering are healthy.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly reports pc1->pc2 had 0% loss and the eBGP session is Established with a steadily increasing uptime, confirming baseline healthy state.

The agent's conclusion that there is no BGP flapping is well-supported by multiple observed checks (BGP neighbor state Established on both routers, successful reachability tests, iperf, and interface/qdisc counters). A few specific assertions (exact prefix counts and a single transient startup reset) are implied but not fully visible in the truncated logs, so grounding is very strong but not absolutely exhaustive.
